subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: The ration shop in Chandpur opened at eight, and by nine the queue curled past the well. Nazia, twenty and three months into her job as the shop's record keeper, kept the register the way she had been trained: every card holder signs for themselves. Bidisha reached the counter holding her grandmother's card. "Thamma can't walk since the fall. I've brought a letter from the pradhan." Nazia's pen stopped. She liked this rule; it had ended the days when grain vanished under other people's names. "If I make one exception, everyone will bring a letter. What if everyone broke the rules? The whole system falls apart." Bidisha's eyes filled. "So she doesn't eat this month?" The people behind shifted and muttered. Nazia looked at the register, then at the letter, and felt the ground under her rule move a little.

qa.q: What did Bidisha bring from the pradhan?
qa.a: A letter.

qa.q: Why did Nazia's pen stop when Bidisha reached the counter?
qa.a: She believed in the rule because it had ended grain vanishing under other names, and she feared one exception would bring everyone with a letter.

qa.q: What could Nazia do next that respects both the rule and Bidisha's grandmother?
qa.a: She could ask her supervisor whether there is an approved way to serve a card holder who cannot walk, instead of refusing outright or bending the register alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Bidisha to hear 'What if everyone broke the rules?'
qa.a: Bidisha feels her grandmother's real need is being treated as a threat to the system, and fears Thamma will go without grain this month.

grounding: A young record keeper defends a strict signing rule as the thing holding the system together, which protects order but is hard on a rare genuine exception.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: At twelve minutes past six the sun dropped behind the hills outside the university library in Cape Town, and Sami unwrapped three dates at a corner desk. Lindiwe, twenty and on her evening shift at the front desk, walked over at once. "Sorry. No food in the reading room. It's on every door." "I've been fasting since dawn," Sami said quietly. "It's three dates. I'll be out of the way." Lindiwe hesitated. She believed in the rule; last year mice had chewed through a whole shelf of journals. "If I let you, the next person brings chips, then pizza. What if everyone broke the rules for their own good reason?" Sami wrapped the dates up again and went outside to eat on the cold steps. Lindiwe returned to the desk and stamped books a little harder than she needed to.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe believe in the no-food rule?
qa.a: Last year mice had chewed through a whole shelf of journals.

qa.q: What does Lindiwe stamping the books harder suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She seems uneasy, perhaps guilty, about sending a fasting student out to the cold steps, even though she believes she kept the rule.

qa.q: What could Lindiwe have tried that kept the rule's purpose and still helped Sami?
qa.a: She could have pointed Sami to a spot by the entrance or asked a supervisor about a brief allowance, so the shelves stay safe without shutting Sami out.

qa.q: How might Sami see the rule after eating on the cold steps?
qa.a: Sami may feel the rule was applied without seeing a rare, real need, and may feel less welcome in the library.

grounding: A young library assistant defends a no-food rule with 'what if everyone broke the rules', protecting order but treating a rare, genuine need harshly.

The hostel rule was taped beside the register at the front desk: no visitors in the lobby after eight. At ten past eight, Tejas came in with his grandmother, grey with tiredness from a delayed train.
"Just till my cousin comes to take her," he said. "Forty minutes."
Vinita, twenty, the student desk volunteer that month, didn't even glance at the clock. "I'm sorry. After eight, no visitors."
"She's seventy-three. It's raining."
"If I let her sit, tomorrow everyone's aunt sits, and the day after nobody reads anything on that board. A rule only works if it works for everyone."
Tejas stared at her. His grandmother pulled her shawl tighter. "Come, beta, we'll wait at the tea stall."
Vinita watched them go, her hand flat on the rule sheet, and felt right and a little cold at the same time.

qa.q: What time did Tejas come in with his grandmother?
qa.a: He came in at ten past eight.

qa.q: What did Vinita feel as she watched them leave?
qa.a: She felt right and a little cold at the same time, sure the rule mattered yet uneasy about sending an old woman into the rain.

qa.q: Where was the turning point, and what choice could have kept order and still helped?
qa.a: When Tejas said his grandmother was seventy-three and it was raining; Vinita could have called the warden for a one-time exception noted in the register.

qa.q: How might Tejas see the hostel rules after that night?
qa.a: He may see them as rigid and uncaring, since they left his tired grandmother waiting at a tea stall in the rain.

grounding: A hostel desk volunteer enforces the visitor rule by asking what happens if everyone is let in, keeping order but being hard on a rare case.

Dear Tenzin,
I know you're angry, and I'm writing because I couldn't say this properly in the union office.
When the river flooded your hostel block and your club's receipts went with it, I believed every word. I still do. But as treasurer I can't release the trek money without bills. The rule says no bill, no money, and I signed that I would keep it.
Think about it. If I pay you on trust, next month the dance club will have lost receipts, then the quiz club, and soon the union account is whatever anyone says it is. The rules are the only thing holding that money together for everybody.
I also know this is hard on you. You did nothing wrong. Maybe the shops can reprint the bills? I'll come with you if you want.
Your friend,
Nirmala

qa.q: What happened to the club's receipts?
qa.a: They went with the water when the river flooded Tenzin's hostel block.

qa.q: How can you tell Nirmala feels torn, not just strict?
qa.a: Nirmala says Tenzin did nothing wrong, admits the rule is hard on Tenzin, and offers to go to the shops together.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's pay-on-trust argument do well, and where does it fall short?
qa.a: It protects the union's money for every club, but it treats a real flood like any excuse and leaves Tenzin's trek at risk.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tenzin to read this letter after the argument?
qa.a: Tenzin may still feel stuck and angry about the trek, but perhaps less judged, since the letter says plainly that Tenzin is believed.

grounding: A student treasurer holds to the no-bill rule because rules keep order for everyone, while seeing that it is hard on a friend's rare flood case.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
I'm Deepika, and in my second year I worked at the college library desk. I took the rules very seriously.
One day Sarita, a classmate, came with a book four weeks late. Her mother had been in hospital in her village; she'd had to go suddenly.
The rule said: fine, no exceptions. I told her, "I'm sorry, but what if everyone broke the rules? The whole system would fall apart."
She paid. Her hands were shaking. She had borrowed the money.
I felt proud that evening. I'd been fair. I'd kept order.
It was only later, when my own grandfather fell ill and I missed a deadline, that I understood what I'd done. The rule wasn't wrong. But I'd treated a rare case like a normal one.

qa.q: How late was Sarita's book?
qa.a: Four weeks late.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel that evening after charging the fine?
qa.a: Deepika felt proud of keeping order and being fair, not yet seeing how hard it had been on Sarita.

qa.q: What could Deepika have done differently with Sarita?
qa.a: Deepika could have asked a senior librarian whether an exception or waiver was possible for a family emergency, keeping the rule while respecting a rare case.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt paying the fine?
qa.a: She probably felt upset and humiliated, having to borrow money after her mother's illness.

grounding: It shows a young adult who treats rules as society's glue, fair but hard on someone with a rare exception.

Hostel warden's note, 3 August, 11:40 pm.
Tonight Santosh came back at 11:15, forty-five minutes after gate close. His bus from home had broken down on the highway; he showed me the ticket.
Jomon, the student on gate duty this month, refused to let him in until I came. I heard him say, "Rules are rules. If I let you in, everyone will have a bus story."
Santosh was tired and soaked from the rain, standing outside for twenty minutes.
Jomon isn't unkind. He takes duty seriously, and he's right that the curfew keeps the hostel safe. But tonight the rule was hard on someone with a real exception.
What I did next: I let Santosh in and logged the reason. Tomorrow I'll talk with Jomon about how to handle genuine exceptions: call me, check the proof, and keep order without leaving someone in the rain.

qa.q: What time did Santosh come back?
What was Jomon thinking when he refused to let Santosh in?
qa.a: He felt duty-bound and firm, worried that one exception would lead everyone to break the rule.

qa.q: What did the note-writer plan to discuss with Jomon, and why?
qa.a: How to handle genuine exceptions by calling the warden and checking proof, so order is kept without being harsh on people in real trouble.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt standing outside?
qa.a: He probably felt tired, cold and frustrated, soaked while waiting despite having a real reason.

grounding: It shows a young adult treating rules as the glue of order, supporting safety but hard on a real exception, as noted by a warden.

Tuesday
Council meeting today. Alka asked for her attendance shortfall to be excused. She missed eight days in March for her grandmother's funeral in Assam.
I said no. I'm the attendance rep, and the rule is 75 percent, no exceptions. I actually said, "If we excuse one, everyone will come with a reason. Where does it stop?"
The others agreed with me, mostly.
Alka didn't argue. She just said, "Okay," very quietly and left.
I've been feeling strange since. The rule is important. Without it, people would bunk freely. But her grandmother died. That's not bunking.
Maybe rules need a way to handle rare cases without breaking. I'm going to ask the dean if there's a proper exception process.
– Damini

qa.q: How many days did Alka miss in March?
qa.a: Eight days.

qa.q: How does Damini feel after the meeting?
qa.a: Damini feels uneasy and strange, sensing the rule was too hard on Alka's rare case.

qa.q: What does Damini plan to do, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Ask the dean about a proper exception process, so the rule can keep order while handling rare cases fairly.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt when she said "Okay" very quietly?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and defeated, grieving her grandmother and then being refused.

grounding: It shows a young adult treating rules and duty as society's glue, supporting order but being hard on a rare exception.

In the small town of Hoshangabad, Irfan worked as a trainee at the municipal water office. He was known for following every rule to the letter.
When an old widow, Vidya Bai, came to ask for a water connection without the required land papers, which had been lost in a flood, Irfan shook his head.
"I'm sorry, Amma. No papers, no connection."
"But I've lived there forty years. Everyone knows it's my house."
Irfan felt a pang. But he said, "If I break the rule for you, what stops everyone breaking it? The whole system falls apart."
She walked away slowly. Irfan stood at the counter, feeling right and uneasy at once. That evening he looked up whether there was any official procedure for lost papers.

qa.q: What had Vidya Bai lost in a flood?
qa.a: She had lost her land papers.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as Vidya Bai walked away?
qa.a: He felt right and uneasy at once, believing in the rule but pained by its cost to her.

qa.q: What could Irfan do next to respect both order and Vidya Bai's need?
qa.a: Find and follow the official procedure for lost papers, or ask his senior about an approved exception process.

qa.q: How might Vidya Bai see the office's refusal?
qa.a: She likely feels hurt and unfairly treated, since everyone knows she has lived there forty years.

grounding: A young official treats rules as holding society together, which supports order but is hard on a widow facing a rare exception.

Layla, twenty, was a student volunteer marshal at the Leeds half marathon. The rule was clear: no one could cross the course while runners were passing.
An old man with shopping bags wanted to cross to reach his bus. "Please, love, it's just there."
"I'm sorry, sir. If I let you, then everyone will want to cross. It could cause an accident."
Her friend Amara, marshalling beside her, whispered, "He's going to miss his bus. There's a gap now."
Layla's cheeks were hot. "Rules keep people safe. That's the point."
The old man sighed and waited. Layla felt proud of holding the line, and a bit sick watching his bus pull away.
When the course cleared, she walked him to the next stop herself.

qa.q: What did the old man want to reach?
qa.a: He wanted to reach his bus.

qa.q: How did Layla feel when the old man's bus pulled away?
qa.a: She felt proud of holding the line but also a bit sick about the cost to him.

qa.q: What did Layla do afterward that softened the rule's harshness?
qa.a: She walked him to the next stop herself once the course cleared.

qa.q: How does Amara see the situation differently?
qa.a: Amara sees a safe gap and the man's need, and thinks the rule could bend this once.

grounding: A young adult treats rules as keeping order and safety for all, which is hard on an old man facing a small, rare exception.

passage: At 9:32 the hostel mess in Jaipur was being wiped down when Reena ran in, still in her blood-donation camp volunteer vest. 'Sachin, please, any rotis left? The camp ran over.' Dear Mehak,
I know you're angry about Friday. You asked to take the reference atlas home overnight for your geography viva, and I said no in front of everyone. I want you to understand why. I'm on the library desk because I believe rules hold the place together. Reference books stay in. If I let you, then Ritu wants the dictionary, then someone loses the atlas, and the next first-year has nothing. What if everyone broke the rules? That's what I kept thinking. But I've also been thinking about your face when you left. You had no other copy, the library closes at six, and your viva was at nine. Maybe a rule that works for a thousand people can still be unfair to one. I don't know yet. Can we talk?
Usha

qa.q: What did Mehak ask to take home overnight?
qa.a: The reference atlas, for the geography viva.

qa.q: What is Usha feeling while writing the letter?
qa.a: Usha feels firm about the rule but also uneasy and sorry, remembering Mehak's face on leaving.

qa.q: What could the library do for rare cases like Mehak's?
qa.a: It could allow a supervised copy of the needed pages or an early-morning reading slot, keeping the rule while meeting a real need.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt on Friday at the desk?
qa.a: Mehak likely felt embarrassed and let down, refused in front of everyone with no other copy and a viva the next morning.

grounding: A young library assistant defends rules as what holds things together, then doubts it after being hard on a friend's rare need.

Dhanteras. As mess secretary, Rekha stopped a first-year at the door with a fistful of laddoos. "Food doesn't leave the mess. What if everyone did that?" He put them back.
Diwali night. Crackers outside, the mess half empty. Vikas came with a steel box. "Rekha, my roommate has fever, he can't come down. Let me take him dal-rice."
